messages.subject: Use names attribute of lists inside a l*ply function
messages.subject_clean: Use names attribute of lists inside a l*ply function
messages.body_plain:
I would like to use in a function passed to l*ply the names attribute
of lists or in the case of lists generated by *lply the values of attr
(,"split_labels"). In the example below that would be the id variables
"first" and "second", but it seems that these attributes are dropped
after l*ply starts processing the lists.

It would be greatly appreciated if somebody could point me in the
right direction, as most probably the list references are not correct.

Thanks.

--
http://learnr.wordpress.com

> library(plyr)
> id <- c("first", "second")
> variable <- c("a", "b")
> df <- expand.grid(id = id, variable = variable)
> dfl <- dlply(df, .(id), data.frame)
> dfl
$first
     id variable
1 first        a
3 first        b

$second
      id variable
2 second        a
4 second        b

attr(,"split_type")
[1] "data.frame"
attr(,"split_labels")
      id
1  first
2 second
> names(dfl)
[1] "first"  "second"
> l_ply(dfl, function(x){print(attr(x,"split_labels"))})
NULL
NULL
> l_ply(dfl, function(x){print(names(x))})
[1] "id"       "variable"
[1] "id"       "variable"

messages.subject_clean: Use names attribute of lists inside a l*ply function
messages.body_plain:
I am working on a report, and am aiming to generate many latex/html
tables using a combination of l_ply and xtable. In order to
distinguish from which list the table was generated it would be nice
to automatically specify the caption argument for xtable which is the
name of the list (a and b in the example below).

a <- data.frame(s1 = c(runif(3)))
b <- data.frame(s1 = c(sample(100,2)))
e <- list(a=a,b=b)

l_ply(e, function(x){
	xtable(x[1])
	}, .print = TRUE)

--
http://learnr.wordpress.com

messages.body_plain:
Ah, in that case I'd use m_ply and explicitly pass in the names:

a <- data.frame(s1 = c(runif(3)))
b <- data.frame(s1 = c(sample(100,2)))
e <- list(a=a,b=b)

library(xtable)
m_ply(cbind(data = e, name = names(e)), function(data, name){
   xtable(data[1], caption = name)
}, .print = TRUE)

Hadley

messages.subject: rbind mlply with id variable
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I often use the following construct with mapply, and I'm trying to
find a cleaner version using plyr,

# define two dummy parameters
a = 3:5
b= letters[1:3]

foo = function(a,b){ # and a dummy function
 data.frame(x=rnorm(1:a), y =rnorm(1:a))
}

tmp <- mapply(foo, a=a, b=b, SIMPLIFY=FALSE) # that would be mlply
(data.frame(a=a,b=b), foo)

names(tmp) <- paste(seq(1,length(tmp))) # assign a unique name to each
data.frame

do.call(lattice::make.groups,  tmp) # rbind the data.frames and create
a unique id

# alternatively (using base R only)

all.names <- do.call(c, mapply(rep, x=names(tmp), each=sapply(tmp,
nrow)))
cbind(do.call(rbind, tmp), which = factor(all.names))

The result looks like this,

|============================
|       | x      | y      | which
| 1.1 | -1.07 | -0.34 | 1
| 1.2 | 0.15  | 0.68  | 1
| 1.3 | -0.18 | 0.42  | 1
| 2.1 | -0.25 | 0.09  | 2
| 2.2 | 0.53  | 1.52  | 2
| 2.3 | -1.65 | -1.16 | 2
| 2.4 | -0.96 | -1.61 | 2
| 3.1 | 0.09  | 0.17  | 3
| 3.2 | 0.01  | -1.07 | 3
| 3.3 | -1.42 | -0.58 | 3
| 3.4 | 0.00  | -0.68 | 3
| 3.5 | -0.28 | 1.15  | 3
|============================

Thanks,

Baptiste

messages.subject: Re: rbind mlply with id variable
messages.body_plain:
Interesting,

this works too (kind of "isplat", or inverse currying),

isplat = function(fun){
  ff <- formals(fun)
if("id" %in% names(ff))
stop("id is part of args(fun)")
  formals(fun) <- c(alist(id=), unlist(ff))
fun
}

a = b  = 3:5
foo = function(a,b){

 data.frame(x=rnorm(1:a), y =rnorm(1:a))
}

isplat(foo)
isplat(isplat(foo)) # error

foo2 = function(a,b,c=3,...){ # testing optional arguments
 data.frame(x=rep(c,length(a)), y =rnorm(1:a,...))
}

 mdply(data.frame(a=a, b=b, id=seq_along(a)), isplat(foo))

 mdply(data.frame(a=a, b=b, id=seq_along(a)), isplat(foo2), c=4, mean=10)

I wonder whether there is a loss in efficiency though (function calls).

Thanks,

baptiste
